questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading the arithmetic of the 1970s
questions.learningObjective: Describe the defining combination of indicators in the 1970s.
questions.stem: Line 1 of the analyst's dashboard shows the 1970s as a decade in which prices climbed while output growth fell and unemployment rose. Which statement best describes the arithmetic of that decade?

options.text: Inflation and unemployment rose together, which the older models said could not happen
The decade proved that price rises always cause faster growth through rising demand
options.misconception: recites the demand story as if it fit the decade

options.text: The decade's arithmetic worked because wages were fixed by law for most of the period
options.misconception: invents a statutory wage freeze

options.text: The decade's arithmetic showed that oil was the only cause of every change in prices
options.misconception: makes oil the single explanation for all price change

questions.explanation: The defining feature of the 1970s was inflation and unemployment rising together, which the classical trade-off denied. Oil shocks were a trigger, not the whole story, and wages were not fixed by law.
questions.hint: Ask what two series did at the same time.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading a worker's strike and its reversal
questions.learningObjective: Read a strike timeline and identify what ended the dispute.
questions.stem: Row 2 of the dashboard note records the British coal strike of 1984 and 1985: a walkout beginning in March 1984, months of confrontation, a ballot among members in March 1985, and a return to work later that month with no national pay settlement. Which reading does that sequence support?

options.text: The dispute ended because the government had agreed a large pay rise with the union leadership
options.misconception: claims a government settlement was reached

options.text: The dispute ended when the strikers themselves voted to abandon it without a settlement
The dispute ended when the mines were nationalised and the strikers were rehired
options.misconception: invents nationalisation as the ending

options.text: The dispute ended when the strike collapsed on the first week of the walkout
options.misconception: moves the collapse to the first week

questions.explanation: The strike was defeated from inside: members voted to end it without a national settlement after the government held out and stockpiled coal. The reversal came from the membership, not from a deal.
questions.hint: Ask who decided that the walkout was over.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reforming a centrally planned economy
questions.learningObjective: Explain why early Soviet reforms failed to change the system's behaviour.
questions.stem: Entry 3 in the analyst's log asks why the first serious attempts to reform the Soviet command economy in the mid-1960s did not stick. Which explanation fits best?

options.text: The reformers wanted to abolish planning entirely, which the apparatus would not accept
options.misconception: misstates the reform aim as abolition of planning

options.text: The reformers lacked the authority to change prices, which sat with the party apparatus
options.misconception: puts price control in the wrong hands

options.text: The reformers changed only enterprise incentives while leaving the plan's output targets intact
The reformers failed because industrial output actually rose every year after the reform
options.misconception: invents rising output as the reason for failure

questions.explanation: The mid-1960s reform kept the state plan and its output targets and only sharpened profit incentives for managers. Because the targets stayed, managers met them and ignored any push to cut costs.
questions.hint: Ask what the reform left exactly as it was.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a border crossing ended a rivalry in 1989
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the crossing of November 1989 was a moment of visibility.
questions.stem: Item 4 on the dashboard card notes the night in November 1989 when crowds crossed a sealed border checkpoint. Explain why that crossing is better described as a moment of visibility than as the cause of the rivalry's end.

answer.exemplar: The wall had been standing for nearly three decades and had already been undermined by economic weakness, the arms race and the new thinking in Moscow, which made clear that the regime in the east would not be backed as before. When a spokesman announced that new travel rules would take effect immediately rather than at some future date, thousands walked to the checkpoints and the guards, unsure of their instructions, opened the barrier. The crossing did not cause the rivalry to end; it made visible what was already under way and removed the last symbol that had held the division in place.

questions.explanation: The crossing expressed a change already under way in Moscow, in the economies and in the alliances. It made the end visible and hard to reverse rather than causing it.
questions.hint: Ask what had already changed before the gates opened.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The agreement to limit missile defenses
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of limiting missile defense systems.

stimulus.body: Note from the analyst's desk: The firm that sells our alarm systems keeps telling us we should stock more of the expensive kind, because a buyer who owns one will never buy a better one. Our insurer says the opposite, that a buyer who owns any alarm at all can stop worrying about the wall. I have told them we will decide when we know who is actually defending the wall, which is not a question either of them is paid to answer.

questions.stem: Note 5 on the analyst's sheet argues that limiting defenses makes deterrence work better. Which historical point does the note correctly support about the agreement to limit missile defenses?

options.text: Limiting missile defenses was meant to make a first strike look survivable to the attacker
options.misconception: reverses the effect of the limit on deterrence

options.text: The agreement fixed the number of offensive missiles that each side could build
options.misconception: mistakes a defensive limit for an offensive one

options.text: The agreement obliged both sides to destroy the radar systems used for early warning
options.misconception: invents a ban on warning radars

options.text: Limiting defenses kept each side's retaliatory force survivable, which is what made deterrence stable

questions.explanation: The logic was that a side which believed its second-strike force could be destroyed would be tempted to strike first. Capping defenses removed that temptation and made the threat of retaliation credible on both sides.
questions.hint: Ask what the limit does to the other side's second-strike force.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Designing a commitment that can be ended
questions.learningObjective: Explain how exit provisions affect the willingness to sign a commitment.
questions.stem: Ticket 6 in the analyst's queue sets two drafts side by side: one agreement with a fixed term and a clause on withdrawal, another with no end date and no way out. Combining the two drafts, which design principle does the pair illustrate?

options.text: A commitment is easier to trust when it can be ended, because neither side must fear being trapped
A commitment is easier to trust when it cannot be ended, because it guarantees continuity
options.misconception: treats permanence as the mark of a trustworthy agreement

options.text: The two drafts show that the length of an agreement matters less than its wording
options.misconception: dismisses the difference between the two drafts

options.text: The two drafts show that withdrawal clauses are used only when a party is already in breach
options.misconception: invents a breach test for withdrawal

questions.explanation: The two drafts trade durability against reversibility. An agreement that cannot be ended binds the parties to terms they might want out of, while one with a withdrawal route is easier to enter but harder to trust.
questions.hint: Ask what each side fears when it signs.

questions.stem: Line 7 of the analyst's dashboard covers the post-war planning for liberated Europe. Which statement best describes the Allied plans in that period?

options.text: The Allies planned a single military administration for all of Germany under one commander
options.misconception: invents a single unified administration for Germany

options.text: The Allies planned zonal occupation, joint control boards and economic recovery to keep the continent stable
The Allies planned to leave European recovery entirely to the domestic governments of each country
options.misconception: denies outside recovery aid

options.text: The Allies planned a single European customs union to begin as soon as the war ended
options.misconception: places a customs union in the immediate post-war plans

questions.explanation: The wartime plans organised occupation in zones run by joint control boards, and recovery aid assumed Europe's economy could not be left to chance. A customs union came later, and in Europe.
questions.hint: Ask what the plans had to cover besides fighting.

questions.topic: Soviet occupation and eastern alignment
questions.learningObjective: Read a dated sequence and describe how eastern alignment was built.
questions.stem: Row 8 of the dashboard note lists the Soviet steps in eastern Europe: troops remaining in the region after the war, friendly governments installed in five countries, a bloc information agency in 1947, an economic council in 1949, and a mutual defence treaty in 1955. Which conclusion does that sequence support?

options.text: The eastern alignment was built from the start as a formal military alliance
options.misconception: jumps straight to a military alliance in 1945

options.text: The eastern alignment grew mainly from economic aid sent to the region after 1948
options.misconception: replaces politics with economic aid

options.text: The eastern alignment was built in stages, from occupation to political control to formal alliance
The eastern alignment existed only after the western alliance was created in the 1950s
options.misconception: ignores the sequence that began with occupation

questions.explanation: The dates show a staged construction: occupation first, then dependent governments, then bloc organizations, and finally the mutual defence treaty. Each step hardened the alignment.

questions.stem: Entry 9 in the analyst's log asks why the oil price rose from roughly three dollars a barrel in 1973 to around ten dollars a year later. Which effect best explains the damage to economies in the West?

options.text: The rise raised the cost of heating oil only, leaving other fuel prices unchanged
options.misconception: limits the effect to heating oil

options.text: The rise changed the trade balances of oil exporters but not of oil importers
options.misconception: claims importers were unaffected

options.text: The rise reduced inflation because cheaper energy fed into consumer prices
options.misconception: reverses the effect on inflation

options.text: The rise pushed up the costs of transport and production, feeding into inflation

questions.explanation: Cheap oil had held down the cost of moving goods and making things across the Western economies. When it rose several times over, those costs fed straight into prices and squeezed real incomes.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading a worker's strike and its reversal
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a strike with a large majority behind it can be lost.
questions.stem: Item 10 on the dashboard card describes the 1985 vote that ended the British coal strike without a settlement. Explain how the union movement could lose a strike it had started with a large majority behind it.

answer.exemplar: The strike was supported by the membership in huge numbers and lost because those same members eventually judged the costs higher than the prospects. The government refused to concede a national pay settlement, stockpiled coal, and made the industrial relations law stricter, including restrictions on picketing and on the use of union funds. The union leadership, which had been elected on a firm mandate, then put the continuation of the strike to a ballot of the members, and the vote went against continuing, so the strike was called off without the agreement the leadership had been sent out to win.

questions.explanation: A strike rests on members continuing to accept hardship without payoff, so the ballot matters more than the original majority. Government resolve, stockpiles and a harder legal framework eroded that support.
questions.hint: Ask who actually had to keep accepting the hardship.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reforming a centrally planned economy
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a partial economic reform actually changed.

stimulus.body: Note from the analyst's desk: The old factory could not be told how many engines to build, so the plan told it. When we asked for a new product the answer was that no plan existed for it, and the machinery stood idle while the goods were imported. The new arrangement says the plant may keep what it earns and sell abroad on its own account, but the state still decides the ceiling, and the ceiling still decides what happens.

questions.stem: Note 11 on the analyst's sheet describes a plant released from central quotas but still bound by a ceiling. Which historical point does the note correctly support about reform in the Soviet Union?

options.text: Reform could loosen the firm's incentives without removing the state's control of output
Reform in the Soviet Union removed state planning entirely within a few years
options.misconception: reads the reform as the end of planning

options.text: Reform left the enterprise's plan obligations untouched and gave firms more freedom
options.misconception: reverses what the reform changed

options.text: Reform succeeded because the state raised the output ceilings it set for each plant
options.misconception: misstates the direction of state control

questions.explanation: The note captures the typical reform bargain: enterprise autonomy was granted in exchange for accepting a state ceiling on output. The command system loosened at the margin without being dismantled.
questions.hint: Ask what the plant still could not do on its own.

questions.learningObjective: State the intended effect of the 1972 missile defense accord.
questions.stem: Line 13 of the analyst's dashboard marks the 1972 accord that limited defensive missiles on each side. Which statement best captures what the limit was intended to achieve?

options.text: It was meant to slow the arms race by limiting the number of radar installations
options.misconception: reduces the accord to a radar limit

options.text: It was meant to make the two alliances adopt a common command structure
options.misconception: invents a joint command arrangement

options.text: It was meant to keep each side's retaliatory force intact, so neither would be tempted to strike first
It was meant to give the side with more bombers a clearer path to disarmament

questions.topic: Designing a commitment that can be ended
questions.learningObjective: Compare a term-limited agreement with a permanent one.
questions.stem: Row 14 of the dashboard note compares two draft agreements: the first runs for a fixed term with a review and a stated exit; the second has no term, no review and no exit. Which conclusion is best supported by the comparison?

options.text: The first draft is stronger because a fixed term obliges both sides to renew the deal
options.misconception: treats a fixed term as a guarantee of renewal

options.text: The second draft is stronger because it cannot be abandoned by either side
options.misconception: confuses permanence with strength

options.text: Both drafts are equally credible because the parties intend to honour them either way
options.misconception: assumes good faith settles the question

options.text: The second draft reduces the risk of being trapped but raises the risk of being abandoned

questions.explanation: A permanent commitment cannot be escaped, so a party that wants out is stuck and the other gains leverage. A term-limited agreement trades that leverage for the possibility of exit.
questions.hint: Ask which risk each draft carries.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why recovery aid was treated as a political instrument.
questions.stem: Entry 15 in the analyst's log asks why the Allies insisted on relief and recovery programmes for Europe after the war rather than waiting for local governments to recover on their own. Which reason fits best?

options.text: A collapse of European production would have strengthened the appeal of communist parties and the Soviet bloc
European voters would have blamed American planners for the hardship of the recovery years
options.misconception: makes domestic electoral calculation the driving motive

options.text: The relief programmes were the easiest way for the Allies to control foreign elections
options.misconception: invents a scheme for controlling elections

options.text: American firms expected to be paid in relief goods rather than in currency
options.misconception: invents a payment method for American firms

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Soviet occupation and eastern alignment
questions.learningObjective: Explain why eastern alignment was not a set of independent choices.
questions.stem: Item 16 on the dashboard card outlines how Soviet power was established in eastern Europe after the war. Explain why the process is described as an alignment rather than a set of independent national choices.

answer.exemplar: Each eastern government was built with Soviet army presence on the ground and Soviet personnel in the security services, so the new authorities owed their positions to Moscow rather than to local consent. Non-communist ministers were pushed out when they resisted, as in Czechoslovakia in February 1948, and the trade and information bodies of the bloc then locked the economies together. The result was not a set of countries that happened to agree, but a system in which the parties in power were chosen with Soviet approval and stayed in power with Soviet support.

questions.explanation: Alignment here means shared leadership chosen under Soviet pressure and sustained by Soviet force, plus bloc institutions that tied the economies together. The parties in power depended on Moscow for their positions.
questions.hint: Ask who the new governments depended on to stay in power.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why the 1970s figures challenged the older economic expectations.

stimulus.body: Note from the analyst's desk: The report says the basket of goods we buy cost 5.7 per cent more in 1970 and 13.5 per cent more in 1980, and that the country produced less at the end of the decade than at the start. My grandfather would say you cannot have both of those at once. I have stopped arguing with the older economics and started reading the table twice.

questions.stem: Note 17 on the analyst's sheet asks a reader to accept two things at once. Which historical point does the note correctly support about the arithmetic of the 1970s?

options.text: Rising prices and rising unemployment together proved the older economic models correct
options.misconception: claims the old models were vindicated

options.text: Rising prices and weak growth together defeated the older expectation of a stable trade-off
Falling prices and rising output together described the decade's arithmetic
options.misconception: reverses both series in the note

options.text: Rising prices and rising output together showed that the decade was prosperous
options.misconception: confuses price growth with output growth

questions.explanation: Prices up sharply while output grew poorly was the decade's signature, and it is what broke confidence in the old trade-off. The old expectation was that one would push the other the other way.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The agreement to limit missile defenses
questions.learningObjective: Explain how limiting defenses can strengthen deterrence.
questions.stem: Item 21 on the dashboard card examines the accord that limited missile defenses. Explain how limiting defenses can strengthen deterrence rather than weaken it.

answer.exemplar: Deterrence depends on both sides believing that striking first is pointless, because the other side can still answer. The 1972 accord capped the anti-missile systems each side could build, which meant neither could expect to destroy the other's retaliatory force in a first strike. Because the survival of the second-strike force became an assumption rather than a hope, the incentive to strike first weakened on both sides, and the same arrangement that limited defensive hardware strengthened the credibility of the threat behind deterrence.

questions.explanation: Capping defenses removes the belief that a first strike could be decisive, so neither side gains from going first. Deterrence rests on that symmetry, not on the size of any defensive system.
questions.hint: Ask what each side gained from the other's survivable force.

stimulus.body: Note from the analyst's desk: The container contract we signed with the shipper runs three years and says either of us may walk away on ninety days notice if the trade route changes. We both prefer the shorter deal, and both of us know exactly what it is worth.

options.text: Longer agreements are always more valuable because they remove the need for renegotiation

options.text: Only parties that expect to breach an agreement ask for a way out of it

options.text: A withdrawal route makes an agreement easier to enter because it lowers what each side risks
The exit clause exists only to protect the party that is already in breach
options.misconception: confuses an exit clause with a breach remedy

questions.explanation: The note shows a bilateral bargain in which both sides price the possibility of walking away. An exit clause lowers the cost of entering, which is what makes agreements that must survive decades possible at all.
questions.hint: Ask what the exit clause does to the other side's willingness.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reforming a centrally planned economy
questions.learningObjective: Explain why loosening rules for firms did not repair the Soviet economy.
questions.stem: Item 27 on the dashboard card sets out the reform programme begun in the Soviet Union in 1985. Explain why loosening the rules for firms did not by itself repair the economy.

answer.exemplar: Reformers in the Soviet Union from 1985 loosened the rules for state firms, allowed cooperatives, and later tried to let enterprises set their own prices, but the state still owned the means of production and still set the plan's main targets. Without a market to clear prices, a price that was set by an official remained a price by decree, and firms had no reason to cut costs, improve quality or find buyers. The political opening that accompanied the reform was at least as important, because it exposed the failures that earlier administrations had covered up.

questions.explanation: Reform of incentives inside a command system does not create the price signals that a command system suppresses. Without them, firms continued to meet targets and ignore costs.
questions.hint: Ask what set prices once the rules were loosened.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading the arithmetic of the 1970s
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the 1970s are treated as an economic puzzle.
questions.stem: Item 33 on the dashboard card sets out the arithmetic of the 1970s for a general audience. Explain why the decade is usually used as the standard example of an economic puzzle rather than a simple success story.

answer.exemplar: The 1970s are cited because the numbers refused to behave as the textbooks said they must. Consumer prices rose by several times over the decade, output growth was weak or negative in several years, and unemployment in the major Western economies roughly doubled from its position at the start. The old models said that rising prices should push unemployment down, because expensive labour would be dismissed and output would adjust. Both series rising together was therefore treated as an anomaly, and the decade forced a rethink of how wages, expectations and productivity interact when governments try to hold down prices that have already begun to rise.

questions.explanation: The decade is the standard puzzle because inflation and unemployment rose together, which contradicted the expected trade-off. That contradiction is why the period reshaped how governments thought about policy.
questions.hint: Ask which two series moved the wrong way.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Allied plans for liberated Europe
questions.learningObjective: Explain why recovery policy involved European institutions.
questions.stem: Item 39 on the dashboard card examines the plan to rebuild a liberated Europe. Explain why recovery policy was designed to involve European institutions rather than only outside agencies.

answer.exemplar: Aid administered entirely by outside agencies would have kept decisions in the hands of the donor and left the continent's own institutions unused, which in practice weakened the political case for the programme. The alternative was to build recovery through European bodies: an organisation of European states to coordinate the aid, and later arrangements that tied particular industries together under joint management. The aim was partly economic and partly political, because a Europe that administered its own recovery would have reasons to keep the cooperation going after the money stopped, and would also have a stronger voice in its own economic decisions.

questions.explanation: Routing recovery through European institutions kept decisions closer to the recipients and gave them reason to maintain cooperation when aid ended. Outside administration alone risked making the programme temporary and paternal.
questions.hint: Ask what would happen to cooperation when the aid stopped.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The agreement to limit missile defenses
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the 1972 accord reads as prudence rather than capitulation.
questions.stem: Item 45 on the dashboard card asks why the 1972 accord on missile defenses is read as an act of prudence rather than as an admission of weakness. Explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: It is tempting to read a limit on defensive systems as a sign that one side had been frightened by the other's capability. The record points the other way. The limit was small, and both sides accepted it, which suggests that neither was seeking a breakthrough in defences at all. What the restriction achieved was the preservation of a mutual fear: each side stayed certain that the other's retaliatory force would survive any first strike, and that shared certainty is what kept the peace between the two forces for the rest of the decade.

questions.explanation: The limit was mutual and small, and its effect was to keep both sides certain their retaliation would survive. That shared certainty is what makes the accord read as prudence rather than capitulation.
questions.hint: Ask what each side knew about the other's second strike.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of partial reform inside a command economy.

stimulus.body: Note from the analyst's desk: The factory I audited last month had been given permission to set its own prices for two products and told to keep the old ceiling on everything else. The manager had the books open on the desk and a list of goods he could not make at all, because the ceiling was below the cost of the parts. Permission to choose did him no good while the cost of making anything stayed in the hands of the state.

questions.stem: Note 51 on the analyst's sheet describes a firm given freedom over prices but not over costs. Which historical point does the note correctly support about reform in a centrally planned economy?

options.text: Partial reform can give firms choices that are meaningless while the state still fixes the underlying costs
Reform of this kind usually fails because the managers lack the will to use it
options.misconception: blames the managers for the failure

options.text: The reform worked because the state had already stopped setting the costs of production
options.misconception: contradicts the note

options.text: The reform was blocked because the state withdrew all price control from the firm
options.misconception: reverses the direction of control

questions.explanation: The note shows the limit of reform inside a command economy: a manager free to set a price cannot act if the cost of the parts is set for him. Choices matter only if administered prices are addressed too.
questions.hint: Ask what the manager still could not control.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a border crossing ended a rivalry in 1989
questions.learningObjective: Explain the dispute over responsibility for the night of November 1989.
questions.stem: Item 52 on the dashboard card examines the border crossing of November 1989. Explain why contemporaries argued over whether the night was a victory for the crowds or a decision taken by the authorities beforehand.

answer.exemplar: Both readings were supported by the facts, and the dispute was about where responsibility lay. The authorities had announced a travel rule that took effect at once, and the announcement itself implied that the government no longer intended to hold the line; the crossing that followed made that intention impossible to reverse, and the guards on duty opened the barrier without any instruction to do so. From that angle the crowd forced the pace and the authorities followed. From the other angle the decision had been made and published before a single person reached the checkpoint, so the crowds confirmed a policy rather than made one, and the pressure that caused the announcement came from the weakness of the position rather than from the people in the street.

questions.explanation: The question is whether the crowd forced a decision or confirmed one already taken and published. Both readings fit, and the answer depends on which moment you treat as the cause.
questions.hint: Ask what the announcement of the new rule implied.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The agreement to limit missile defenses
questions.learningObjective: Combine the missile defense accord with the other limits of the 1970s.
questions.stem: Ticket 53 in the analyst's queue pairs the missile defense accord with the later armoured and missile treaties of the 1970s. Combining them, which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The defensive accord was the only one of the three that both sides actually observed
options.misconception: claims the defensive limit alone was broken

options.text: The defensive accord showed that limits on weapons could not be verified in practice
options.misconception: generalizes about verification from one case

options.text: The three agreements together removed the possibility of surprise attack on the retaliatory forces
options.misconception: overstates what the agreements could guarantee

options.text: The agreements reduced the incentives to strike first by making each side's survivable force the rule

questions.explanation: Taken together, the agreements of the decade left both sides with an assured retaliatory force and with less to gain from going first. None of them removed surprise entirely, and each had its weaknesses.
questions.hint: Ask what the limits did to the incentive to strike first.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Designing a commitment that can be ended
questions.learningObjective: Compare the trade-off between reversible and permanent commitments.
questions.stem: Line 54 of the analyst's dashboard compares a fixed-term agreement with one that can be renounced on notice. Which statement best captures the trade-off between them?

options.text: A reversible agreement is easier to sign, while a permanent one is easier to rely on
A reversible agreement is stronger because the parties can always adjust to events
options.misconception: assumes reversibility adds strength

options.text: A permanent agreement is easier to sign because it commits the parties from the outset
options.misconception: assumes permanence removes the problem of entry

options.text: The two designs differ only in the length of the notice period required
options.misconception: ignores the difference in the underlying obligation

questions.explanation: An exit clause lowers the cost of committing, which makes agreements reachable; but reliance is easier when terms will not change under the other side. Designers have to choose a point on that trade-off.
questions.hint: Ask which draft is easier to sign and which is easier to rely on.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Allied plans for liberated Europe
questions.learningObjective: Read the stated concerns behind the Allied occupation plans.
questions.stem: Row 55 of the dashboard note lists the concerns behind the Allied occupation plans: preventing a revived German military threat, keeping the economy supplied enough to avoid unrest, and building institutions that could take over later. Which reading does that list support?

options.text: The plans were written chiefly to extract resources from the occupied territory
options.misconception: makes extraction the stated purpose

options.text: The plans tried to hold a dangerous region together while preparing a way out of occupation
The plans assumed the occupation would last for several decades
options.misconception: assumes a decades-long occupation

options.text: The plans gave priority to punishing the defeated population
options.misconception: misreads the plans as punitive

questions.explanation: Occupation was a holding arrangement: the aim was to keep order and supply without provoking a new crisis, while building institutions that could take over. That is a plan with an exit built into it.
questions.hint: Ask what the plans were preparing for.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Soviet occupation and eastern alignment
questions.learningObjective: Describe how eastern alignment was consolidated after the occupation years.
questions.stem: Entry 56 in the analyst's log asks how eastern alignment was consolidated after the initial occupation years. Which answer best fits the record?

options.text: By holding joint elections in which non-communist parties were permitted to win seats
options.misconception: invents competitive elections in the east

options.text: By negotiating a mutual defence treaty with the western alliance in the early 1950s
options.misconception: invents a defence agreement with the west

options.text: By creating bloc organisations for information and trade and by a mutual defence treaty in 1955
By admitting the eastern states to equal membership of the United Nations
options.misconception: misstates the eastern states' standing in the United Nations

questions.explanation: Consolidation came through institutions: a bloc information agency, an economic council for coordinated planning, and in 1955 a mutual defence treaty. These made the alignment a structure rather than an arrangement of convenience.
questions.hint: Ask what the new institutions did for the alignment.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading the arithmetic of the 1970s
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the inflation and unemployment series of the 1970s together.
questions.stem: Row 57 of the dashboard note compares the decade's inflation and unemployment series: prices rose several times over while unemployment roughly doubled from its level at the start of the decade. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The two series moved together, which the older models of the period said could not happen
options.misconception: describes the outcome the models denied

options.text: Unemployment fell as prices rose, which is what the older models predicted
options.misconception: states the old prediction as if it occurred

options.text: Prices fell while unemployment rose, so the decade was a period of cheap money
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the price series

options.text: Prices and unemployment rose together, which is why the decade is called one of stagflation

questions.explanation: Rising prices together with rising unemployment is the combination that defines the decade, and it broke the expected trade-off. The name for the condition comes from exactly those two movements.
questions.hint: Ask what the two series did in the same years.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading a worker's strike and its reversal
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the defeat of the 1984 to 1985 coal strike was a turning point.
questions.stem: Item 58 on the dashboard card asks why the defeat of the British coal strike of 1984 and 1985 is treated as a turning point rather than a routine industrial dispute. Explain what the defeat changed.

answer.exemplar: The defeat mattered less for the settlement, of which there was none, than for what it showed about the balance of power. A government had refused a demand that the most powerful union in the country had previously expected to win, had kept essential supplies moving through a stockpile, had changed the law to restrict the dispute, and had then let the union's own members vote on whether to continue. That sequence made it possible for governments to believe that a strike could be weathered, and it reshaped the strategy of unions across the country in the years that followed, including the extensive deindustrialisation and the closure of pits that reduced the industry's strength.

questions.explanation: The defeat demonstrated that a government could outlast a powerful union and then let its members decide. That changed the calculation for both sides in later disputes.
questions.hint: Ask what the vote made possible for later disputes.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reforming a centrally planned economy
questions.learningObjective: Identify the incentive obstacle at the heart of command economy reform.

stimulus.body: Note from the analyst's desk: The trouble with the plant is not the rules on the floor. It is the office at the top that decides what the floor should make before anyone asks the floor. Give the managers their freedom and they still bring us the same plan, because that is what is in their bonus. Change the bonus and the office above them will simply issue a smaller plan and a harsher one. Nobody here is paid to ask what the buyer would actually buy.

questions.stem: Note 59 on the analyst's sheet identifies the deeper obstacle to reform. Which historical point does the note correctly support about reforming a centrally planned economy?

options.text: Reform fails mainly because managers resist new rules imposed from above
options.misconception: blames managers for resisting reform

options.text: Reform works when the state raises the number of targets given to each plant
options.misconception: suggests more targets would improve performance

options.text: Reform must change what managers are rewarded for, because the state's targets shape their incentives
Reform is impossible in any economy where the state owns the means of production
options.misconception: generalises to an absolute claim about ownership

questions.explanation: The note locates the obstacle in incentives set from above: managers are rewarded for meeting the plan, so reform of rules alone changes nothing. Changing what the system rewards is the deeper reform.
questions.hint: Ask what the managers are paid to do.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a border crossing ended a rivalry in 1989
questions.learningObjective: Combine the 1989 crossing with the preceding change in Soviet policy.
questions.stem: Ticket 60 in the analyst's queue pairs the night of the border crossing with the changes in Soviet policy that preceded it. Combining them, which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The changes in Soviet policy were a response to the crowd at the crossing
options.misconception: reverses cause and effect

options.text: The crossing was the visible point at which a policy already under way became irreversible
The crossing had no effect because the eastern authorities had already lost all control
options.misconception: overstates the loss of authority

options.text: The crossing marked the moment Soviet policy changed direction for the first time
options.misconception: misplaces the moment of the policy change

questions.explanation: The policy had already shifted; the crowd at the checkpoint turned a settled change into an accomplished fact. That is why the night is remembered as the moment the rivalry ended.
questions.hint: Ask what the crowd changed that the policy had not.
